newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka telecom deal seen boosting economy.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka telecom deal seen boosting economy.

text.p: Sri Lanka's decision to sell a stake in its telecommunications monopoly to Japan's Nippon Telephone and Telegraph Corp (NTT) on Tuesday was welcomed by market analysts as a much needed boost to the economy.
"It represents a major step taken by the government in terms of its commitment to hand the reins of the economy to the private sector," brokerage Jardine Fleming said in a report.
Sri Lanka on Tuesday announced a landmark deal under which it sold 35 percent of Sri Lanka Telecom (SLT) and management to NTT for $225 million.
The government will hold the remaining 65 percent.
Government officials said it was the biggest single foreign investment in the Indian Ocean island.
Sri Lanka is selling loss-making public enterprises to improve its creaking infrastructure and attract foreign investment.

Telecom's sale was seen as a major test for the government, which has in recent months sold most of the state-owned plantations companies and plans to sell off part of the equity and management in national carrier Air Lanka.
Jardine Fleming said it had revised the government's budget deficit forecasts for 1997 after the Telecom deal.

The brokerage said in a report that it had lowered its budget deficit forecast to 7.2 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP) from an earlier 8.2 percent. The deficit in 1996 stood at 8.9 percent of GDP.

The government had targeted to raise only five billion rupees ($85 million) through privatisations in 1997, but analysts said that was achieved through sales of plantations and other smaller state firms.
Dushyantha Wijayasinghe, research manager at Asia Securities, said a short-term benefit of Telecom's sale should be a stable, low interest rate regime.
"The government could redeem a substantial percentage of its treasury bill holdings, now standing at about 125 billion rupees, and reduce pressure on interest rates," he said.
Nanda Nair, research director of brokerage John Keells, said the country would benefit from the technology transfer that NTT would make in developing SLT.
"Direct investments from NTT are not going to stop with $225 million either, because they will invest more money on expansions," he said.
NTT is expected to increase the number of telephone lines substantially under the deal.
Analysts said the Colombo Stock Exchange would benefit when a percentage of SLT's share capital of 1.8 billion 10-rupee shares was floated on the market.
Officials said the government might eventually want to reduce its holding to some 51 percent and float the remaining shares on the market within about three years.
"It will be an enormous issue and will hugely improve Colombo's market capitalisation and liquidity," Nair said.
